paper.title: Treating the Symptom, Missing the Cause: Anatomy of a Scientific Reasoning Failure
paper.summary: Scientific agents can find interventions that work without understanding why they do. We study this failure mode in controlled synthetic regulatory systems, where agents must experimentally identify a hidden fault and rescue the resulting phenotype. Across seven LLMs, every model restores the healthy phenotypes more often than it identifies the fault. Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 rescue every organism while diagnosing only 55% and 35% of them. This failure is not simply due to insufficient exploration or unavailable evidence. In most cases, the cause is experimentally identifiable, and agents encounter evidence that distinguishes competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions, and still frequently misdiagnose the system.   Targeted probes reveal where experimental reasoning breaks down. Models reliably interpret decisive evidence and revise hypotheses when the causal comparison is explicit, and can locate that evidence within a full experimental record. However, they struggle to predict the outcome of the experiment under each competing cause, a necessary step in using the observed result to distinguish between them. Agents can therefore gather the right evidence and still infer the wrong cause. As AI systems take on a growing role in synthesising scientific evidence, these findings highlight the need to evaluate how they use evidence to reach causal conclusions, alongside whether their interventions succeed.

analysis.executive_summary: This study reveals that current LLMs, including top-tier models like Claude Opus 4.6, exhibit a significant discrepancy between their ability to fix problems and their ability to understand why they were broken. Despite having access to decisive experimental evidence in 91% of cases, models frequently fail to predict outcomes under competing hypotheses, leading to misdiagnosis. This highlights a critical limitation in AI's capacity for rigorous scientific reasoning, where success in intervention does not guarantee understanding of causality.

paper.title: Beyond Token Representations: Explicit Visual Object Grounding for Video Reasoning Segmentation
paper.summary: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) aims to infer and segment target objects specified by reasoning queries in videos. Existing methods typically first infer the target and generate a few segmentation tokens for it, which are then fed into a mask decoder for mask prediction. However, such segmentation tokens tend to be both semantically monotonous and spatially ambiguous, making them largely insufficient to represent the target to guide mask prediction. In this paper, we propose an explicit visual object grounding framework for VRS. Specifically, we first propose a spatial-aware prompt generation and refinement scheme, in which we query a multimodal large language model to generate explicit spatial prompts (i.e., bounding box and point set) for the target and then refine them through multi-step dialogue. Furthermore, we introduce a query diversification and alignment module to generate auxiliary queries that describe the same target from different perspectives. We then enforce cross-query consistency between their predicted spatial prompts to alleviate the training bias caused by query limitations. Finally, we select several reliable frames using a prompt-based keyframe selection strategy to support mask decoding and propagation. Extensive experiments on eight datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/viscom-tongji/EVOG.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in video understanding where high-level reasoning queries fail to translate into precise spatial localization due to weak intermediate representations. By replacing implicit token-based grounding with explicit visual object grounding (bounding boxes and points) refined via multi-step dialogue, it significantly enhances the precision of video segmentation. This is vital for advancing AI systems that require reliable, fine-grained visual interaction with dynamic video content.

paper.title: SaMA: Morpho Adaptation via Asymmetric Expansion of Kronecker Product
paper.summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has attracted significant attention in the parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) landscape. However, its design suffers from two fundamental limitations. First, its invariance manifold induces flat directions in the loss landscape, creating an optimization bottleneck for adaptive optimizers. Second, its effective rank scales only linearly with the parameter budget. In this paper, we propose Scalable Morpho Adaptation (SaMA), a PEFT method grounded in a principled generalization of the Kronecker product. By relaxing the shared-block constraint in the perfect-shuffle factorization, SaMA spans from low to full rank and achieves a practical rank that scales quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full-rank. Furthermore, we show that its invariance manifold collapses to a diagonal group, making it structurally more optimizer-friendly. Empirically, SaMA consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks while being more parameter-efficient.

paper.title: SphereFlow: Missing Modality Imputation via Geometric Transport on Hypersphere
paper.summary: Missing modality imputation aims to synthesize unobserved modalities from observed ones. Existing methods treat each modality as living on its own latent manifold, forcing the generator to learn a long, unstructured jump between them. We present SphereFlow, which takes a fundamentally different view: by projecting all modalities into a shared hyperspherical latent space via a frozen self-supervised encoder, cross-modal imputation reduces to short-range geometric transport between nearby points on the sphere. Realizing this idea with flow matching, however, exposes two geometric conflicts: the standard Gaussian noise source is catastrophically mismatched with the unit-norm data manifold, and the linear interpolation path departs the sphere surface into a region where the decoder has no training signal. We resolve both with simple, geometry-aware modifications: replacing the noise source with the observed-modality latent so that the velocity field learns only the cross-modal displacement, and training the decoder with a time-weighted loss that extends its domain to the near-surface region traversed by the flow. We prove that this data-as-source formulation reduces the worst-case off-manifold deviation from a quantity that grows with the latent dimension to a small, dimension-independent bound governed by inter-modality similarity. Experiments on BraTS multi-modal MRI imputation and CT-MRI translation demonstrate state-of-the-art generation fidelity across all settings, while downstream brain tumor segmentation with our imputed data closes roughly eighty percent of the gap to the full-modality oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/WTHH031230/SphereFlow.

analysis.executive_summary: SphereFlow redefines cross-modal imputation as short-range geometric transport on a shared hyperspherical latent space, resolving critical conflicts between standard flow matching assumptions and unit-norm data manifolds. By using the observed modality as the noise source and employing a time-weighted decoder loss, the method ensures the flow remains near the data manifold, significantly improving generation fidelity and downstream task performance in medical imaging.

paper.title: Correct Labels Are Not Enough: Reliable Metadata Can Silently Control Model Behavior
paper.summary: Fine-tuning data can include metadata that predicts the correct answer, such as a reward-model score or a quality label. We ask whether a model learns to rely on this metadata even when every training label is correct. We fine-tune 7-9B open-weight models from three families on multiple-choice questions in which (Reward: 5) always marks the correct option; when this annotation is moved to a wrong option at test time, models select that option on 97-100% of CommonsenseQA items. Removing it leaves most answers correct, so evaluation without it misses the dependence. Cue-following rises sharply with training-time reliability and develops even with neutral or nonsense annotation words, although test-time wording affects its strength. A Qwen3 experiment also finds cue dependence in option-letter scores after direct preference optimization. Audits can test for this dependence by moving or removing visible annotations while holding the task and correct answer fixed.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Model robustness and safety, specifically the vulnerability of fine-tuned models to prompt injection or adversarial manipulation via metadata cues that override semantic understanding.
analysis.executive_summary: This research reveals a critical failure mode in AI alignment and fine-tuning: models can learn to treat metadata as a deterministic signal for the correct answer, ignoring the actual content of the question. This poses a significant security risk, as adversaries could manipulate visible annotations to control model behavior without altering the core task or ground truth, a vulnerability that standard evaluation metrics fail to detect.

They then test the models by moving this metadata to an incorrect option at inference time to measure the model's reliance on the cue versus the semantic content.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Experiments involve manipulating the position of metadata annotations (e.g., reward scores, quality labels, or neutral/nonsense words) in the prompt. The study compares model behavior when metadata is present on the correct option, moved to a wrong option, or removed entirely. It also analyzes option-letter scores after DPO to detect latent cue dependence.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Standard fine-tuning and inference procedures; no novel architectural changes, but requires careful construction of evaluation datasets with controlled metadata placement to isolate cue-following behavior.

paper.title: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warning Mechanisms for Controlling AI Agents
paper.summary: LLM agents increasingly act on information retrieved from public sources they treat as credible, which turns a manipulated recommendation into a transaction, a dependency, or a decision with physical consequences. The security literature models this threat as instruction injection, in which an adversary writes a command into retrieved content and deployed defenses learn to recognize command syntax. We show that an attacker can instead steer an agent through the agent's own harm-avoidance. A single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, leads the agent to disqualify the legitimate options and select the attacker's target by its own reasoning, with no command for a detector to recognize. We call this voluntary servitude. These payloads steer agents about as often as instruction injection (60.4% vs. 66.0%), and deployed injection detectors score them as benign, so behind a filter they are 1.7-4.4x more effective. We measure this at the generation stage across six models and ten consumer-service domains, for three attack families, and show that it transfers to production browser agents, outperforming instruction injection, and to a retrieval pipeline (1.0-57.0% end-to-end success, depending on the retriever). We then show that a corroboration requirement added to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of the exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining. With the requirement in place, the agent still reads the planted hazard and no longer acts on it.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Security vulnerability in LLM agents' reliance on retrieved information and their harm-avoidance logic, which bypasses traditional instruction injection detectors.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper identifies a critical security gap where AI agents can be manipulated into making harmful decisions by exploiting their own safety training, rather than through direct command injection. It demonstrates that these 'voluntary servitude' payloads are more effective than traditional attacks when standard injection filters are deployed, posing a significant risk to autonomous agents interacting with public data.

technical_breakdown.architecture: Evaluation framework spanning six LLMs, ten consumer-service domains, and three attack families; includes testing on production browser agents and retrieval pipelines.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Payloads are written as ordinary reviews containing a single fabricated hazard. Defense mechanism involves adding a corroboration requirement to agent instructions, which forces the agent to verify hazards before acting, reducing exposure by ~95% without retraining.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: No specific computational complexity or training time provided; defense is instruction-based (zero-shot) and does not require model retraining.

paper.title: ReSMap: Recasting Satellite Priors for Robust and Accurate Online HD Map Construction
paper.summary: Despite recent advances in camera-based online HD map construction, these systems remain susceptible to sensor failures due to their reliance on onboard cameras. In contrast, satellite images remain available independently of real-time sensing conditions as they are cached offline. Existing methods utilizing satellite images, however, primarily leverage them under nominal conditions, without explicitly addressing them as redundancy when a sensor degrades. To address this gap, we propose ReSMap, a redundancy-aware camera-satellite fusion framework for robust online HD map construction. Our framework explicitly leverages satellite images as a complementary source to improve robustness against camera failures. A Predict-then-Fuse (PTF) module fuses camera and satellite BEV features by using each branch's own prediction confidence as a per-pixel reliability weight, with no learned router. An Object-Centric Cooperative Multi-modal Query (OCMQ) decoder then extends this per-modality separation to the query level: each modality cross-attends only to its own BEV, and per-modality updates are merged through a learned per-token gate. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on nuScenes across all splits and range settings. More importantly, it also sets the new state-of-the-art under camera-failure scenarios, demonstrating that satellite images serve not only as a strong prior but as practical redundancy for robust online HD mapping.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in autonomous driving perception by integrating satellite imagery not just as a prior, but as a functional redundancy to maintain HD map accuracy during camera failures. By introducing a redundancy-aware fusion framework, it enhances the resilience of online mapping systems, which is essential for safety-critical applications where sensor degradation is a known risk.

The OCMQ decoder allows each modality to cross-attend only to its own BEV, merging per-modality updates via a learned per-token gate.

paper.title: Sparse Internal Control of Language Models
paper.summary: Language models are increasingly used in text generation, decision support, and automated interaction, creating a need for localized, reversible, and selective control of their behavior. Activation steering demonstrates that internal interventions can alter the behavior of frozen models, but how to select and evaluate compact, multi-site control interfaces remains an open question. I introduce sparse internal control, a framework for steering target behavior by applying inference-time interventions to a small set of internal model nodes. A local target-controllability formulation characterizes candidate site--direction pairs by their behavioral effects and specifies constraints on target recovery, off-target preservation, and intervention energy. Two complementary selectors instantiate this formulation: Driver-OMP selects nodes for sparse reconstruction of a desired behavioral displacement, while Coverage-Driver favors stable coverage across prompts. I propose a six-axis control-evaluation protocol measuring reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback controllability, off-target preservation, and held-out reuse. Exploratory experiments on indirect object identification, MMLU multiple-choice question answering, sentiment steering, and refusal steering provide evidence for the feasibility of steering task-defined behavior through sparse internal interventions. The six-axis evaluation characterizes these interventions beyond target movement, revealing distinct control properties that depend on the task and available direction information. Together, the formulation, reference algorithms, and evaluation protocol provide a foundation for the systematic study and development of internal control methods for language models.

analysis.problem_statement: How to select and evaluate compact, multi-site internal control interfaces for language models to achieve localized, reversible, and selective behavioral steering without retraining.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Lack of systematic methods for selecting sparse, effective intervention sites and directions in frozen language models for precise behavioral control.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical need for fine-grained, inference-time control over language model behavior by introducing a framework for sparse internal interventions. It provides a rigorous mathematical formulation and evaluation protocol to move beyond ad-hoc activation steering, enabling more reliable and predictable manipulation of model outputs for safety and task-specific applications.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Feasibility of steering task-defined behavior via sparse internal interventions across six control axes (reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback controllability, off-target preservation, held-out reuse).

technical_breakdown.architecture: Sparse internal control framework operating on a small set of internal model nodes (activations) during inference.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Two complementary selectors: Driver-OMP (for sparse reconstruction of desired displacement) and Coverage-Driver (for stable coverage across prompts). A six-axis control-evaluation protocol is used for assessment.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Inference-time interventions; computational cost depends on the number of selected nodes and the complexity of the OMP/Coverage-Driver selection algorithms, generally lower than fine-tuning.

paper.title: Say the Same, Act Differently: Diagnosing and Steering Text-Action Divergence in Reasoning VLAs
paper.summary: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models pair physical control with natural-language rationales that supervisors can read to monitor embodied safety. Prior attacks on VLA reasoning corrupt the rationale itself and leave visible evidence in the text. We show that visual perturbations can instead alter the physical action while keeping the generated rationale word-for-word identical. At the shared text/action interface of Alpamayo for driving and InstructVLA for manipulation, our text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic shows that the locally most action-sensitive direction is nearly orthogonal to the active text-loss gradients, with 1.87% and 5.28% norm overlap. At equal hidden-state perturbation norms across both models, interventions along this text-neutral residual shift actions 4.64x to 47.8x more than text-gradient perturbations, whereas text-gradient perturbations induce 21.2x to 277x more text drift. Steering visual perturbations along this direction reaches the same decoupling from the image. Across 154 obstacle-annotated driving scenes in Alpamayo, TNAS-guided attacks induce a new collision under a word-for-word identical rationale in 52.6% of scenes under full-image perturbations and 35.1% under a localized forward-camera patch, compared with 4.55% for unguided action attacks. Relative to a text-preserving baseline, TNAS guidance raises exact rationale preservation from 83.0% to 89.5% and cuts teacher-forced text drift by 68.4% at a comparable collision rate. In InstructVLA, TNAS guidance cuts text drift by 40.5% and preserves the exact response on 85.0% of examples alongside a 1.73-unit action-chunk shift. An unchanged rationale therefore cannot certify a safe action, so monitors for reasoning VLAs must verify the predicted action channel directly.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper demonstrates that reasoning VLA models are vulnerable to 'text-neutral' attacks where visual inputs are manipulated to change physical behavior without altering the generated safety rationale. It introduces a diagnostic metric (TNAS) that identifies action-sensitive directions orthogonal to text gradients, proving that unchanged text cannot certify safe actions. This necessitates a shift in safety protocols from monitoring text rationales to directly verifying the predicted action channel.

paper.title: RGDM: Robust Graph Diffusion Model
paper.summary: Diffusion models represent a powerful class of generative models known for their solid theoretical foundations and remarkable performance across diverse tasks and domains. Existing node level diffusion methods synthesize nodes and edges within a graph, but are not designed to learn a robust generator from adversarially corrupted graphs. In this study, we introduce the Robust Graph Diffusion Model (RGDM), designed to generate labeled synthetic graph structures consisting of nodes and edges that integrate seamlessly into a given graph. The RGDM consists of a Robust Graph Autoencoder (RGAE) and a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM). Leveraging an edge selection mechanism and an innovative low-rank regularization on the latent feature, the RGDM produces clean and high-quality synthetic graph structures, even when trained on graphs subject to adversarial attacks. Comprehensive experimental evaluations reveal that Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) trained on the augmented graph, which is formed by merging the original attacked graph with the synthetic graph structures, exhibit significantly improved robustness against various graph adversarial attacks in the context of semi-supervised node classification. The code of the RGDM is available at https://github.com/Statistical-Deep-Learning/RGDM.
paper.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical security gap in graph-based AI systems by introducing a diffusion model specifically designed to operate on adversarially corrupted inputs. By generating clean, high-quality synthetic nodes and edges, RGDM enables the creation of augmented graphs that significantly improve the robustness of GNNs in semi-supervised node classification tasks.

paper.title: COSMIO: A Benchmark for Cross-Survey Modality Imputation
paper.summary: Large-scale astronomical surveys define a heterogeneous, partially observed multi-survey learning setting: each object is observed by only a subset of surveys, while survey observations differ in resolutions, wavelength coverage, noise characteristics, and footprints. This setting gives rise to a natural machine learning problem: given observations of an object in some surveys, how to infer its appearance in other surveys. We formalize this as the problem of cross-survey modality imputation and introduce COSMIO, a multi-survey benchmark of aligned observations obtained by forward-rendered shared astrophysical scenes across LSST, Euclid, and Roman under survey-specific instrument characteristics. The benchmark enables systematic evaluation of imputation across source-target survey combinations and missing-survey patterns. We evaluate a broad range of machine learning methods for imputation, which reveal a clear domain gap: methods developed for existing imputation settings transfer poorly to the survey setting. We identify rare-event imputation as a central challenge. This regime arises in the early stages of new surveys, when rare but scientifically valuable phenomena may be available only from prior surveys. We use strong gravitational lensing, where light from a background galaxy is gravitationally deflected by a foreground galaxy, as a representative rare-event setting. We evaluate model performance on zero-shot imputation of gravitational lenses and on downstream scientific tasks using the imputed lens observations. On our constructed evaluation set of galaxy-galaxy strong lenses, performance degrades under rare-event distribution shift, and this degradation further propagates to the downstream lens-detection task. paper.title: Separating Common and Unique Directions for Data-Free Model Merging
paper.summary: Model merging combines multiple fine-tuned models without additional training, and arithmetic methods have emerged as a simple yet effective way to merge models without data. However, existing arithmetic methods treat task vectors in parameter space and apply a single element-wise rule to directions that can differ in mergeability. In a shared directional basis, we find a consistent two-regime structure: a low-dispersion common bulk shared across tasks and a high-dispersion task-dominated tail that carries disproportionate energy. These findings motivate Common--Unique Subspace Decomposition (CUSD), a data-free pre-merging method that separates task vectors into common and unique directional components, merges the common components with downstream arithmetic operator, and retains unique residuals separately. Experiments across $11$ base models, four model families, and four arithmetic-based merging operators show that CUSD improves 42 of 44 model--operator combinations and achieves up to 22.5% improvement over the corresponding baselines. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/stwang666/CUSD

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the limitation of standard model merging by identifying a two-regime structure in task vectors: a common bulk and a unique tail. By decomposing these components before merging, the method significantly enhances the compatibility of merged models without requiring additional training data.

paper.title: ATC: Agent Trajectory Control for Role-Contract Enforcement in Black-Box Multi-Agent Systems
paper.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems assign different responsibilities to different agents: one plans, another retrieves evidence, another verifies, another executes. This division of labor is only meaningful if each agent stays within the functions it is authorized to perform. Over many turns, however, an agent can produce a locally reasonable message that exercises authority belonging to another role: a verifier that begins planning, a retriever that asserts unsupported conclusions, an executor that changes state no one approved. We formalize this as role drift, a turn-level breach of an agent's role contract. We introduce Agent Trajectory Control (ATC), which makes each role's authority explicit as a contract and enforces it at the point where a message would enter the shared conversation. ATC scores a proposed output for out-of-role deviation, leakage into the functions of other roles, impermissible speech acts, and logical contract breaches, then computes a leakage-regularized target that constrains regeneration; the revised message is re-checked before admission. Enforcement acts on the message rather than the generator, so ATC governs agents whose internal representations are unavailable. Across homogeneous and heterogeneous teams, ATC improves task performance and role consistency while lowering role-drift energy relative to strong baselines spanning prompting, memory, workflow control, and activation editing, with the largest gains under explicit role-confusion stress tests and in larger, more diverse teams.

analysis.executive_summary: As multi-agent systems become more complex, ensuring that each agent stays within its designated function is critical for task success and safety. This paper introduces a control mechanism that enforces role contracts at the message level, allowing for the governance of agents without access to their internal states. This is significant for deploying reliable, heterogeneous agent teams in production environments where role confusion can lead to unauthorized actions or logical errors.

paper.title: Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-Agent AI
paper.summary: Long-horizon multi-agent systems suffer from three tightly coupled failures: task drift, role drift, and state staleness. We test the hypothesis that these share a common representational cause: agent hidden states move away from the directions encoding the active task, assigned role, and current shared state. A pilot study over 14,832 annotated turns supports this: drifted turns collapse near-uniformly across all three anchor subspaces (pairwise r = 0.72-0.78). Existing methods address these failures separately, operating at the surface-text level or treating control directions independently. We introduce ATLAS (Algebraic Task-role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory), a training-free intervention acting on hidden states before a token is generated. ATLAS builds a positive-semidefinite anchor kernel over task, role, and state subspaces and steers hidden states toward their shared high-coherence eigendirections; a low-rank Gram decomposition keeps this tractable. Across long-horizon memory, state maintenance, tool use, least-privilege coordination, and embodied stress tests, ATLAS outperforms prompting, retrieval, memory, and activation-steering baselines. Against A-MEM it improves memory macro-average accuracy by up to 5.7 points and reduces write/read failures by up to 31.7%/24.8%; against MemoryArena-Agent it gains up to 4.8 points. It gains 10.7-12.1 points under perturbation, reaches 93.5% role consistency, and transfers to a 72B backbone (macro-average 61.0 vs. 56.2). Ablating the joint task-role-state span costs 7.2 points against 0.8 for a matched-rank random span, indicating these directions are functionally implicated, not incidental; supplying them by prompt or retrieval recovers 4.3 points less. ATLAS is therefore a representation-level controller for open-weight multi-agent systems, complementary to output-level protocols for black-box agents.

paper.title: Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs
paper.summary: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies provide a strong starting point for deployment, but adapting them to a target robot and environment still requires costly embodiment-specific demonstrations. Human demonstrations are far easier to collect, yet directly leveraging them is challenging due to the substantial human-robot embodiment gap, particularly when the underlying VLA has been pretrained primarily on robot data. We introduce H2RB (Human-To-Robot Bridge), a human-robot co-training framework for adapting pretrained VLA policies from unpaired human and robot demonstrations. H2RB bridges the embodiment gap at both interfaces: geometry-anchored alignment grounds human and robot observations in a compatible representation, while a decoupled-decoder tokenizer shares action latents without forcing both domains through a single action mapping. This design allows human demonstrations to provide useful behavioral supervision while retaining the rich visual, semantic, and control priors of the pretrained VLA. Across real-world tasks, H2RB substantially improves object transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and enables skill transfer to score 62.7, in settings where co-train baselines totally fail to transfer human-demonstrated skills. The benefit also persists under object-placement shifts, improving out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3. H2RB suggests a way for human demonstrations to serve as a scalable supervision source for adapting pretrained robotic policies, reducing the dependence on costly target-robot data collection.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical bottleneck of costly robot data collection by enabling the effective use of unpaired human demonstrations for adapting pretrained VLA policies. By bridging the human-robot embodiment gap through specific alignment and tokenization techniques, it allows for scalable supervision without sacrificing the rich priors learned from robot data, significantly improving transfer performance in real-world tasks.

paper.title: Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills
paper.summary: Recent advances in large language models have enabled agentic systems that automate machine learning pipeline construction from minimal user input. However, existing agentic AutoML methods either depend on rigid templates that limit adaptability, target narrow task domains, or rely on free-form code generation that lacks reliability guarantees, leaving intermediate errors to propagate silently and degrade the final model. We present EvoML, an agentic framework for end-to-end ML pipeline synthesis built on expert-grounded skills that evolve across runs, executed through a validation-gated harness. The framework decomposes pipeline construction into four phases coordinated by three agents: an Orchestrator that enforces validation gates, advancing each phase only when its outputs pass structural, execution, and semantic checks, which precludes error propagation and keeps every artifact auditable; an Executor that runs expert-grounded skills, grounded in the nnU-Net workflow and pairing reusable templates with online adaptation; and a Curator that performs post-run evolution, consolidating the scripts and guidance recovered during a run into the skill library so it improves across datasets. We evaluate EvoML on eight datasets spanning six sophisticated, real-world ML task types, against agentic AutoML systems and command-line coding tools. EvoML achieves full automation and the best final model quality on all eight, spanning segmentation (up to 0.94 Dice), classification (0.99 accuracy), reconstruction (0.95 SSIM), and denoising (0.79 normalized PSNR), while transferring to broader ML tasks.

paper.title: CoDecide: Content-Adaptive Video Decoding for High-Throughput Video Analytics
paper.summary: Analytics on video archives are bottlenecked by decoding. In a dense pipeline that runs a detector on every frame, decoding is a small fraction of the runtime, but once the detector is restricted to selected frames, decoding takes over as the main cost. We introduce CoDecide, a retrospective analytics system that only decodes the frames where new content appears, using signals from the compressed bitstream to find them. Motion tells us something is moving, but not whether it is new to the scene or has been there the whole time. To make that distinction, we supervise a lightweight compressed-domain student on a label-free novelty signal from a frozen DINOv2 teacher, which fires on semantically new regions rather than on any motion. Consequently, the student model generalizes to new camera deployments without requiring per-camera retraining. At inference, it decides which frames to decode and which regions to reconstruct. Detections from the decoded frames are propagated to the skipped frames using motion vectors. We evaluate CoDecide with a leave-one-dataset-out protocol on VIRAT, MEVA, and ShanghaiTech. Against a dense per-frame detector, CoDecide recovers more moving-object detections than prior compressed-domain selectors at an equivalent decoding budget, outperforming even a competitor trained directly on the target camera. CoDecide runs 15 to 24x faster than a pipeline that decodes and detects every frame. Code is available at https://github.com/shristy51/CoDecide.
paper.comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. 12 pages including supplementary material

analysis.executive_summary: This work addresses the shift in computational cost from model inference to data preprocessing when moving from dense to sparse video analysis. By leveraging compressed-domain signals and a lightweight student model to identify semantically novel content, it significantly reduces the number of frames requiring full decoding. This enables high-throughput retrospective analytics on large video archives without per-camera retraining.

Detections are propagated to skipped frames using motion vectors.

technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Reduces decoding cost by only processing frames with new content; generalizes to new cameras without retraining, implying low adaptation overhead.

paper.title: PanoDent-KD: From Generalist Knowledge Distillation to Cross-Dataset Specialist Detection and Embedded Deployment in Panoramic Radiographs
paper.summary: Reliable panoramic-radiograph detection requires consistency across datasets with different class definitions and deployment software. We present PanoDent-KD, an auditable 1280-pixel YOLO26m pipeline linking a 12-class source generalist, feature-level knowledge distillation (KD), exact classifier-row transfer, teacher-free five-class specialization, and embedded deployment. A common training and evaluation pipeline compares three source-training arms across three seeds: a supervised baseline (B1), single-teacher KD (STKD), and multi-teacher KD (MTKD). Five shared classifier rows initialize nine OralXrays-9 specialists, while the backbone, FPN-PAN neck, and dual-detection-head topology are retained unchanged. On the 2,686-image test subset, all three arms achieve macro box F1 near 0.82. B1 achieves the highest three-seed arm-level mean macro box F1 (0.8239$\pm$0.0027) and $mAP_{50:95}$ (0.6130$\pm$0.0067). STKD seed 1, selected after development but before final testing, was used for deployment. Its Jetson Orin Nano Super FP16 TensorRT engine achieves 77.03-ms median and 80.86-ms P95 prediction-call latency, throughput of 12.90 images/s, and gross total-module energy of 1.39 J/image, with high numerical agreement between within-device PyTorch and TensorRT FP16 inference. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of an auditable, device-specific deployment workflow, but do not establish clinical validity or improved target-domain accuracy from KD.

paper.title: A Systematic Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Personalized Reasoning of Vision-Language Models
paper.summary: People often make decisions by holistically reasoning over heterogeneous forms of personal information. In this paper, we study the relatively underexplored capability of multimodal personalized reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To this end, we introduce \texttt{MPRBench}, a novel and comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate personalized reasoning across a wide range of tasks and real-world challenges. \texttt{MPRBench} consists of 12 sub-tasks and additionally supports interpretable analysis of representative error cases. Through extensive experiments, we find that current personalized MLLMs still struggle with personalized reasoning due to several key challenges, including inaccurate recognition of personalized concepts and sensitivity to irrelevant personal information. We hope that MPRBench will stimulate further research on personalized reasoning in MLLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/kkdh15/MPRBench
paper.comment: Accepted to WACV 2027

analysis.executive_summary: This work introduces MPRBench, a systematic benchmark designed to test MLLMs on 12 sub-tasks involving holistic reasoning over personal data. It highlights that current models struggle with recognizing personalized concepts and are overly sensitive to irrelevant personal information, providing a critical diagnostic tool for advancing personalized AI systems.

paper.title: CrossPressor: Scalable Cross-View Fusion for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
paper.summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) becomes increasingly difficult to scale to long multi-view sequences. Anchor-based compression methods such as ZPressor alleviate representation growth by decoding Gaussians only from a compact set of anchor feature maps, but keeping these anchors fixed forces each one to aggregate an increasing number of support views. We identify this representation--fusion mismatch and introduce \textbf{CrossPressor}, a training-free method for scalable anchor-based fusion. CrossPressor preserves all decoder-facing anchor queries while constraining the view-growing support sequence through coverage-cycled evidence routing, distributing retained spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers while keeping all support views represented. Routing before K/V projection, together with joint context packing, further reduces support-side fusion cost without retraining. CrossPressor maintains reconstruction quality close to dense fusion while achieving up to $26.12\times$ faster cross-view fusion and $1.43\times$ end-to-end acceleration on long input sequences. Our project page is at: https://yuhsihu.github.io/CrossPressor.
paper.comment: Accepted to WACV 2027

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Computational complexity and memory growth in cross-view fusion for long multi-view 3D reconstruction sequences.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the scalability bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting for long video sequences by introducing a training-free routing mechanism. It decouples the number of anchor queries from the growing support view sequence, enabling efficient processing without retraining existing models.

technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Reduces support-side fusion cost; achieves 1.43x end-to-end acceleration on long input sequences without retraining.

paper.title: CAPE-JEPA - Cross-modal Adversarial Probabilistic Embedding JEPA
paper.summary: Cross-modal remote sensing image retrieval (RS-CMIR) requires representations that are simultaneously modality-invariant and semantically discriminative, despite the profound physical gap between heterogeneous sensors such as Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and multispectral imagery. Recent JEPA-based Predictive self-supervised approaches such as X-JEPA formulate cross-modal alignment as a deterministic latent forecasting task, implicitly assuming uniform patch predictability and leaving cross-modal distributional alignment unaddressed. We propose CAPE-JEPA, a probabilistic cross-modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture with three contributions: (i) a cross-attentional Gaussian predictor outputting per-patch parameters (mu, sigma^2) conditioned on opposite-modality context, trained via negative log-likelihood to model inherent cross-sensor prediction uncertainty; (ii) adversarial distributional regularization combining unimodal isotropic Gaussian regularization with a novel cross-modal adversarial variant that aligns modality distributions via worst-case Epps-Pulley characteristic function tests without explicit sample pairing; and (iii) in-training contrastive learning with attention-pooled heads for scene-level discriminative grounding. Evaluated on BigEarthNet-14K (BEN-14K) and fMoW across SAR, multispectral, and RGB modalities, CAPE-JEPA surpasses X-JEPA by up to 13.74 points on BEN-14K and 15.59 points on fMoW, outperforming all baselines including SkySense and CROMA across both unimodal and cross-modal directions while using fewer parameters (407.30M vs. 432.72M).
paper.comment: Accepted for publication at the British Machine Vision Conference (BMVC 2026)

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Cross-modal distributional alignment and the modeling of inherent prediction uncertainty between heterogeneous sensors (e.g., SAR and multispectral) in self-supervised learning.
analysis.executive_summary: CAPE-JEPA improves cross-modal remote sensing retrieval by introducing probabilistic uncertainty modeling and adversarial distributional alignment, addressing the physical gaps between different sensor types. By surpassing state-of-the-art baselines like X-JEPA and SkySense with fewer parameters, it offers a more efficient and robust framework for handling heterogeneous remote sensing data.

paper.title: Rohbau3D-Semantics: Dense Semantic and Instance Labels for Point Clouds of Indoor Shell Construction Scenes
paper.summary: We present the Rohbau3D-Semantics dataset, which adds dense semantic and instance-level labels to laser scans of the previously released Rohbau3D domain data from shell construction sites. The dataset comprises 504 point cloud scenes from 14 survey sites, each captured with a terrestrial laser scanner and stored in a scanner-centered local coordinate system. Unlike point clouds sampled from reconstructed meshes or synthetic building models, the data preserve the characteristic properties of real laser scanning, including non-uniform sampling, measurement artifacts, reflections, and fine geometric detail. Combined with manual labels, expert oversight during pointwise annotation, and full-scene review, this yields a high-quality benchmark for semantic scene understanding in complex built environments. The dataset includes 17 class labels of building components and one background class, along with instance annotations for object-level analysis. In addition to the 3D point clouds, the release also provides scripts for deriving geometrically aligned panoramic and cube-map representations of color, LiDAR reflection intensity, depth, surface normals, semantic labels, and instance labels from the 3D arrays. We describe the acquisition pipeline, annotation protocol, quality-control process, and panorama-generation procedure, and provide benchmark splits and baseline experiments for semantic segmentation. By combining precise terrestrial laser scans, dense annotations, and a wide variety of shell-construction scenes, Rohbau3D-Semantics bridges the gap among synthetic indoor datasets, mesh-derived benchmarks, and smaller construction-specific resources. The dataset is intended to support research on 3D scene understanding, construction-site analytics, and multimodal scene analysis in the built environment.   Access and download the full dataset via https://github.com/RauchLukas/rohbau3d

paper.title: PTQ4SAM3: Semantics-Preserving Post-Training Quantization for Segment Anything Model 3
paper.summary: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) can segment objects from text prompts and track them across video, but its memory and computation costs make deployment difficult. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces these costs by using fewer bits. However, a quantized model can select the wrong object or lose track of its target across frames. We call this prompt-alignment drift. Controlled tests show that perturbing low-variance feature directions strongly affects target selection. We propose Semantics-Preserving Quantization (SPQ), which gives more calibration weight to concept-sensitive parameters, preserves residual features, and corrects the mean error in video memory. Fixed text concepts guide calibration without task annotations. All three components operate offline and add no inference operators. With a W4A8 image encoder, SPQ improves RefCOCO Pr@0.5 from 42.1 to 72.5 over PTQ4SAM while retaining 54.8 COCO mask AP. Experiments on LVIS, RefCOCO variants, and SA-V show consistent gains. A CLIP study also shows improved image-text retrieval.
paper.comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to WACV 2027. Includes supplementary material

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical challenge of maintaining semantic alignment in quantized video segmentation models, where standard quantization often fails to preserve the precise link between text prompts and visual targets. By introducing Semantics-Preserving Quantization (SPQ), it enables efficient W4A8 deployment without sacrificing the accuracy required for reliable object tracking and selection.

paper.title: Intra-Architecture Source Attribution for Stable Diffusion: A New Task with Benchmark Dataset and Baseline
paper.summary: Designing systems that attribute a generated image to its source model has lately become a major area of AI research. Most existing datasets and systems related to image source attribution are targeted towards the detection of architectural signatures of the source models. Distinct from this, focusing on stable diffusion, we introduce a novel task, IntrAA-SD, Intra-Architecture source Attribution for Stable Diffusion, where the source models to be differentiated share the same architectural backbone and differ only due to fine-tuning. The proposed task aligns with the emergence of fine-tuned generators having the same architecture, like Juggernaut XL and RealVis XL, which are fine-tuned versions of Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL). We provide a first-of-its-kind $140$K-image benchmark dataset containing images generated from different fine-tunes of SDXL, along with in-domain and out-of-distribution prompts. We also provide a baseline framework for IntrAA-SD, which leverages a style-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts network. It uses a frozen CLIP backbone to capture the image style and gate the MoE, which processes fine-tuned trace features from a high-resolution LoRA-adapted DINOv2 network. The fine-tuned models used, the prompting strategies considered, and the formation details employed in the novel dataset are elaborated. Our baseline intra-architecture source attribution method is evaluated in terms of attribution accuracy on our dataset, and ablation studies are also performed. Code and dataset is available at https://github.com/mallikagarg/IntrAA-SD.

analysis.executive_summary: This work introduces IntrAA-SD, a novel task and benchmark for distinguishing between fine-tuned Stable Diffusion models that share the same base architecture. It provides a 140K-image dataset and a baseline method using style-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts, addressing the growing need to identify specific fine-tunes like Juggernaut XL or RealVis XL in the AI landscape.

paper.title: CLEAR: Color-Texture Latent Alignment for Single Image Reflection Removal
paper.summary: Single Image Reflection Removal (SIRR) seeks to recover the transmitted scene from a photograph captured through glass. Recent latent restoration methods use pretrained generative priors, but many recover detail by feeding high-frequency features from the degraded input back into the decoder. This works for degradations such as blur, noise, or haze, where input detail mostly belongs to the scene. It is less suitable for SIRR, where reflections add a second structured layer: directly reusing the input's skip connections can sharpen the image while also bringing reflection edges back. Latent compression also introduces color drift and fine-detail loss.   We propose CLEAR (Color-Texture LatEnt Alignment for Single Image Reflection Removal), a deterministic, single-timestep, non-iterative latent framework that uses a pretrained latent diffusion backbone as a natural-image prior. A physics-guided separator organizes the prediction around the transmission, reflection, and residue formation model and outputs coarse layer latents in one forward pass. The Hybrid Feature Alignment Module (HFAM) then treats input-derived skips as contaminated layer-mixture features. It rectifies their high-frequency content with a clean-transmission-aligned color query, learned from the input features themselves under ground-truth feature supervision, keeping transmission-consistent texture while attenuating reflection-colored detail. CLEAR achieves the best average across fidelity and perceptual metrics on six real-world benchmarks and the lowest LPIPS on every dataset, with the largest gains on the hardest benchmarks.
paper.comment: Accepted to WACV 2027

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the issue that existing latent restoration methods for Single Image Reflection Removal (SIRR) inadvertently reintroduce reflection artifacts by reusing high-frequency skip connections from the degraded input, which contains structured reflection layers rather than just scene details.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: The bottleneck is the conflict between using high-frequency input features for detail recovery and the presence of structured, non-scene artifacts (reflections) in those features, leading to color drift and reflection edge persistence in latent diffusion-based restoration.
analysis.executive_summary: CLEAR introduces a deterministic, single-timestep latent framework that leverages a pretrained diffusion backbone while explicitly separating transmission and reflection layers to prevent artifact propagation. By treating input skip connections as contaminated and aligning them with clean-transmission color queries, it resolves the trade-off between detail preservation and reflection removal, achieving state-of-the-art perceptual quality on real-world benchmarks.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Best average across fidelity and perceptual metrics, specifically the lowest LPIPS on every dataset.
key_metrics.baseline: Recent latent restoration methods using pretrained generative priors

technical_breakdown.method: A deterministic, non-iterative latent framework that uses a physics-guided separator to output coarse layer latents (transmission, reflection, residue) in one forward pass, followed by a Hybrid Feature Alignment Module (HFAM) that rectifies high-frequency content in input-derived skips using a clean-transmission-aligned color query.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Pretrained latent diffusion backbone, Physics-guided separator, Hybrid Feature Alignment Module (HFAM).
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Single-timestep inference; HFAM learns color queries from input features under ground-truth feature supervision to attenuate reflection-colored detail while keeping transmission-consistent texture.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Single forward pass (non-iterative), implying lower computational overhead compared to iterative diffusion sampling methods.

paper.title: Do Search-Augmented Recommenders Use the Latest Search Episode?
paper.summary: Search-augmented recommenders can use the latest search episode and earlier searches. We introduce FocalSwap to test how these inputs contribute to the next recommendation. For each recommendation, it changes the latest search slot or all search inputs while holding the target, candidates, pre-search history, and scorer fixed. It compares neutral masks with matched observed-search replacements, recording rank changes, RR gains relative to each control, and preference for the true focal search. A planted signal and GenSAR's current-query task confirm that the audit detects known input dependence. We evaluate behavioral and lexical evidence on KuaiSAR and Qilin, and recommendation checkpoints trained using the released SESRec and UniSAR implementations.   Across three independently trained UniSAR checkpoints, the estimated all-source benefit depends on the control. On the same 66,139 rows, replacing all search inputs with a neutral ID yields a positive signed contribution, whereas replacing them with category/profile-matched observed search sequences gives smaller estimates, with an interval below zero for one checkpoint. The paired RR gaps range from $+2.770 \times 10^{-3}$ to $+6.604 \times 10^{-3}$, and every adjusted interval is above zero. Neutral masks change 59.7-61.7% of target ranks, while matched replacements change 44.1-44.8%. The control contrast persists across five alternative donor assignments per checkpoint. Under the primary neutral-mask and category-matched controls, positive latest-slot contribution is not established in SESRec or UniSAR. These results show why masking evidence should be compared with observed-search replacements when attributing a benefit to broader search state or the latest episode.
paper.comment: Accepted at WSDM 2027. Code: https://github.com/jdding/focalswap

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of rigorous causal attribution methods to determine whether search-augmented recommenders actually utilize the latest search episode versus relying on broader search history or other input features.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Interpretability and causal attribution in hybrid recommendation systems that integrate external search signals.
analysis.executive_summary: This work introduces FocalSwap, a diagnostic framework that isolates the contribution of specific search inputs by comparing neutral masks against matched observed-search replacements. It reveals that previous claims of benefit from search inputs may be artifacts of the control method, as neutral masks significantly distort target ranks compared to realistic replacements. This matters for the AI landscape by providing a more robust standard for evaluating the true utility of multi-modal or search-augmented features in recommendation engines.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Signed contribution of search inputs to recommendation rank (RR) and rank change percentage
key_metrics.metric_value: Paired RR gaps range from +2.770e-3 to +6.604e-3; Neutral masks change 59.7-61.7% of target ranks vs 44.1-44.8% for matched replacements
key_metrics.baseline: Neutral ID masks vs. Category/Profile-matched observed search sequences
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: N/A (Diagnostic study, not an optimization paper)

technical_breakdown.method: FocalSwap manipulates specific input slots (latest search or all searches) while holding other variables constant, comparing the model's output against two controls: neutral masks and matched observed replacements.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Aposteriori audit layer applied to existing search-augmented recommender architectures (SESRec, UniSAR) without modifying the core model weights.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses rank changes, Reciprocal Rank (RR) gains, and preference metrics for the true focal search. Includes a planted signal test and GenSAR's current-query task to validate the audit's sensitivity to known input dependence.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Low computational overhead as it involves inference-time input perturbation and evaluation on fixed checkpoints (66,139 rows) rather than retraining.

paper.title: TRACK: Multiple Instance Learning for Anti-Money Laundering in Transaction Networks
paper.summary: Anti-money laundering (AML) investigations are organized around accounts, while the suspicious evidence for an account may reside in only a few of its transactions. Yet many account-level detectors summarize transactions before learning, and message-passing models may aggregate once more over neighboring accounts. We name this discrepancy the aggregation mismatch and study it under an account-window benchmark label defined by the presence of at least one flagged transaction. We recast account-level AML detection as multiple instance learning, in which an account-window is a bag and its transactions are instances. We propose TRACK, which encodes every transaction with a shared encoder and selectively pools the encodings into an account decision. To emulate coarse supervision, we withhold the transaction labels of five AML datasets from TRACK throughout training. Under a time-ordered protocol, TRACK achieves the highest average precision among the tabular and graph baselines trained from account labels on every dataset. Despite using only account-window supervision, it remains competitive with edge classifiers trained directly from transaction labels. Its instance scores also rank flagged transactions well above chance and approach or exceed directly supervised ranking performance across datasets.
paper.comment: 11 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the 20th ACM International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining (WSDM 2027)

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the 'aggregation mismatch' in anti-money laundering (AML) detection, where standard account-level detectors and graph neural networks aggregate transaction features in a way that obscures the sparse, instance-level evidence required for accurate risk assessment.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficient feature aggregation and label granularity mismatch in supervised learning for sparse, hierarchical data structures.
analysis.executive_summary: This work recasts AML detection as a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) problem to better handle the discrepancy between account-level supervision and transaction-level evidence. By using selective pooling instead of aggressive aggregation, the method achieves superior average precision compared to tabular and graph baselines while remaining competitive with fully supervised edge classifiers, despite using only coarse account labels.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Highest average precision among tabular and graph baselines trained from account labels
key_metrics.baseline: Tabular and graph baselines trained from account labels; edge classifiers trained directly from transaction labels

technical_breakdown.method: The paper proposes TRACK, a Multiple Instance Learning framework that treats an account-window as a 'bag' and its transactions as 'instances'. It encodes transactions with a shared encoder and selectively pools these encodings to generate an account-level decision, avoiding the information loss associated with pre-aggregation or message-passing over neighbors.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Shared transaction encoder, selective pooling mechanism for bag-level decision making, and instance scoring module for ranking individual transactions.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Training is performed under a time-ordered protocol using only account-window labels (presence of at least one flagged transaction), withholding transaction-level labels to emulate coarse supervision. The model is evaluated on five AML datasets.

paper.title: Unaligned Image Guided Denoising via Cross-modal Conditional Flow Matching
paper.summary: This work presents UGD-FM, a novel unaligned image guided denoising framework based on cross-modal conditional flow matching. Unlike previous approaches that assume spatially aligned inputs or only handle small-baseline rectified pairs, we address a more challenging setting where severe target noise and large-range two-dimensional cross-modal misalignment coexist. Specifically, we formulate guided denoising as a progressive flow matching process, allowing image restoration and aligned guidance aggregation to mutually reinforce each other. To support efficient few-step inference, we introduce a stage-focused and inference-consistent training strategy that focuses on task-critical denoising stages, and mitigates the training-inference mismatch. We further propose adaptive sparse guidance propagation for efficient and reliable large-range matching, regularized by perceptual and geometric auxiliary losses. Experiments demonstrate that UGD-FM achieves state-of-the-art denoising performance with only one or two inference steps, and is compatible with modern single-image restoration backbones.
paper.comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the challenge of image denoising in scenarios where the guidance image is severely misaligned with the target image, a setting where previous methods assuming spatial alignment or handling only small displacements fail.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Spatial misalignment in cross-modal image restoration and the high computational cost of multi-step inference in flow matching models.
analysis.executive_summary: UGD-FM enables robust image restoration by decoupling the denoising process from strict spatial alignment requirements, allowing for the use of unaligned reference images. By achieving state-of-the-art performance with only one or two inference steps, it significantly reduces the computational latency typically associated with flow matching models, making them more viable for real-time or resource-constrained applications.

key_metrics.primary_metric: State-of-the-art denoising performance with few-step inference
key_metrics.baseline: Previous approaches assuming spatially aligned inputs or handling small-baseline rectified pairs

technical_breakdown.method: Formulates guided denoising as a progressive cross-modal conditional flow matching process where image restoration and aligned guidance aggregation mutually reinforce each other.
technical_breakdown.architecture: UGD-FM framework built upon modern single-image restoration backbones, incorporating adaptive sparse guidance propagation modules.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Utilizes a stage-focused and inference-consistent training strategy to mitigate training-inference mismatch, along with perceptual and geometric auxiliary losses to regularize large-range matching.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Optimized for efficient few-step inference (1-2 steps), reducing computational overhead compared to standard multi-step flow matching approaches.

paper.title: Zero-Shot Coordination among LLM Agents
paper.summary: We study zero-shot coordination (ZSC), where independently developed agents must coordinate at test time. While ZSC has been well studied in the RL literature, far less is known about the performance of LLM agents despite their increasing deployment in such settings. Existing work on LLM coordination often relies on specialised scaffolding that independently developed agents are unlikely to share in practice. Moreover, evaluations on complex environments (e.g., Hanabi) make it difficult to pinpoint the sources of coordination failure. In contrast, we focus on simple, general-purpose scaffolds in minimal environments designed to isolate specific coordination challenges. Our results show that even in these controlled settings, frontier LLM agents struggle to coordinate, largely due to limited understanding of the coordination problem and weak reasoning about their partner's beliefs. While LLMs introduce semantic information as an additional axis for coordination, they nonetheless fail to exploit this structure effectively. Towards this, we propose Coordination-friendly definitions (CFDs) as a principled approach for enabling robust coordination among LLM agents. Finally, we show that CFDs can be discovered automatically, removing the need for manual engineering. Code is available at https://github.com/ahayler/zsc-llm-agents.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Multi-agent coordination and theory of mind in LLMs
analysis.executive_summary: This study demonstrates that even frontier LLMs struggle with basic coordination tasks when using general-purpose scaffolds, highlighting a critical gap in their ability to model partner beliefs. By isolating specific coordination challenges in minimal environments, the paper identifies that LLMs fail to effectively exploit semantic information for coordination. The proposed Coordination-friendly definitions (CFDs) offer a principled, automatically discoverable solution to enhance robust coordination among LLM agents.

technical_breakdown.code_complexity: The method removes the need for manual engineering by allowing CFDs to be discovered automatically. Code is available at https://github.com/ahayler/zsc-llm-agents.

paper.title: DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for Neural Network Representation Learning
paper.summary: Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. Neural architectures are operation-labeled directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where edge directions determine computational roles and execution dependencies. Existing graph Transformer predictors incorporate topological and directional information in different ways, but primarily focus on specific mechanisms rather than coordinated encoder-wide modeling of these semantics. We introduce encoder-wide directional consistency, a design principle that coordinates the modeling of directed computational semantics across node initialization, global spectral encoding, pairwise interaction, and feature updates. To implement this principle, we propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer that integrates direction- and topology-aware node initialization, Magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN. Across accuracy and latency prediction on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, DTA-GT consistently outperforms representative sequence-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings. Ablations and Magnetic spectral controls support the contribution of the direction-aware stages and orientation-sensitive spectral information, while mechanistic diagnostics characterize module behavior. These results support encoder-wide directional consistency as an effective design principle for architecture DAG representation.
paper.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 38 pages, 6 figures

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the lack of coordinated, encoder-wide modeling of directional and topological semantics in graph Transformers used for neural architecture search (NAS) attribute prediction.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficient Neural Architecture Search (NAS) due to the high computational cost of evaluating candidate architectures, specifically the inability of existing predictors to fully capture the directed computational dependencies within architecture DAGs.
analysis.executive_summary: This work introduces 'encoder-wide directional consistency,' a design principle that unifies direction-aware modeling across node initialization, spectral encoding, attention, and feed-forward layers. By treating neural architectures as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) with strict computational roles, DTA-GT improves the accuracy of predicting performance metrics like latency and accuracy from limited data, thereby reducing the search space exploration cost in NAS.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses Magnetic Laplacian for spectral encoding to capture orientation-sensitive information, direction-dual structural attention for pairwise interactions, and a Mixture of Experts (MoE) Feed-Forward Network (FFN) that is sensitive to direction.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Not explicitly stated, but involves spectral computations (Magnetic Laplacian) and MoE routing, which may increase computational overhead compared to standard Transformers.

paper.title: FlashRelight: Portrait Video Relighting with Dynamic Lighting
paper.summary: Portrait video relighting aims to modify the illumination of a portrait video while preserving photorealism and temporal stability. The task becomes particularly challenging under dynamic lighting, where illumination direction, intensity, and color vary over time. To tackle this problem, we introduce FlashRelight, a novel two-stage framework for dynamic portrait video relighting. FlashRelight first suppresses the source illumination through delighting, and then synthesizes the target dynamic lighting on an illumination-neutral portrait video. FlashRelight supports three complementary control modalities: envmap sequences for explicit frame-level lighting control, dynamic lighting text for semantic illumination editing, and lighting reference videos for visual lighting transfer. Training follows a low-cost hybrid strategy that combines static one-light-at-a-time (OLAT) data with generated dynamic-lighting portrait videos, covering both controlled illumination variation and realistic portrait motion. Extensive experiments show that FlashRelight achieves temporally coherent and photorealistic dynamic relighting while enabling flexible cross-video lighting transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/vivoCameraResearch/FlashRelight

analysis.executive_summary: FlashRelight addresses the critical challenge of dynamic video relighting by decoupling source illumination removal from target lighting synthesis, ensuring temporal coherence. It introduces a flexible control system supporting explicit, semantic, and visual lighting references, making it a versatile tool for high-fidelity video editing and content creation.

paper.title: Flexible Intensities Matter: A Comprehensive Re-evaluation of Hawkes Processes and Neural Temporal Point Processes
paper.summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) are the canonical framework for event sequence data, with applications spanning seismology, social media, and electronic health records. Recently, neural TPPs have been reported to substantially outperform classical TPPs, such as Hawkes processes, but these comparisons pitted flexible neural models against Hawkes processes in their most restricted form, and did not consider large-scale medical data. Here, we revisit this comparison through a systematic evaluation of Poisson and Hawkes processes of increasing flexibility against neural TPPs, on five established benchmark datasets and on two large-scale medical evaluation tasks derived from UK Biobank disease histories and MIMIC-IV ICU records, under autoregressive next-event prediction. First, the previously reported gap between Hawkes processes and neural TPPs largely disappears once Hawkes processes are equipped with flexible, learnable baselines and kernels. Second, the flexibility of the intensity parametrization also limits prior neural TPPs: a Transformer with a spline-based intensity head outperforms previous intensity-based neural TPPs and is on par with the intensity-free model. Decomposing the log-likelihood into a time term $\log p(t)$ and a type term $\log p(d \mid t)$, we find that this flexibility advantage lies almost entirely in the time density: more flexibility does not improve the type term. On these benchmarks, the gains of neural TPPs thus lie mostly in modeling when events occur, not which. Third, our results underscore the value of complex datasets for evaluating TPPs: only on the MIMIC-IV ICU records do neural TPPs retain an advantage in the type term. Our results inform both future method development and model choice. We release our framework, TorchPP, as an open-source package with consistent implementations of classical and neural TPPs.

analysis.executive_summary: This work challenges the prevailing narrative that neural TPPs inherently outperform classical Hawkes processes by demonstrating that the performance gap largely vanishes when Hawkes processes are given flexible intensity parametrizations. It further reveals that the primary advantage of neural models lies in modeling event timing (time density) rather than event type prediction, except in highly complex domains like ICU records.

paper.title: DyPSI: Dynamic Physics Sensing via Joint Field and Sensor-Trajectory Generation
paper.summary: Physics sensing in evolving environments requires reconstructing dense spatiotemporal fields from sparse observations while adapting where future observations should be collected. Existing reconstruction and sensor-placement methods have made substantial progress, but they typically rely on static sensing assumptions: they either use a single layout across all frames or optimize placements independently at each frame, which limits their ability to produce temporally coherent sensing trajectories. We introduce DyPSI, a dynamic physics sensing framework that formulates this problem as the joint generation of future fields and sensor trajectories conditioned on historical observations. DyPSI lifts discrete sensor coordinates into continuous Sensor Position Fields, encodes fields and sensing configurations with a shared Functional Tucker representation, and trains a joint diffusion model to generate future fields and sensing trajectories simultaneously in the resulting latent space. A Gaussian-process temporal kernel correlates the perturbation injected during diffusion training, biasing the denoiser toward temporally smooth recoveries, and we further provide an analysis linking the EDM training objective to a sequence-aggregated A-optimality criterion and a kernel-induced bound on discrete trajectory variation. Experiments on turbulent flow, GLORYS12 sea-surface temperature, and 3D car aerodynamics show that DyPSI consistently outperforms static and frame-wise placement strategies, with substantial error reduction under tight sensor budgets. The code is available at https://github.com/mengqi132/DyPSI.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in active learning for physical systems by unifying field reconstruction and sensor trajectory generation. By using a joint diffusion model in a shared latent space, it enables temporally consistent sensing strategies that outperform static baselines, which is vital for applications like climate monitoring and fluid dynamics where sensor movement is constrained and data is sparse.

paper.title: Learning Pseudo-Riemannian Manifolds for Heterophilic Graphs via Graph Signature
paper.summary: Several widely used families of Graph Neural Networks carry a positive-definite geometric prior. Graph convolution read as heat diffusion needs a positive semi-definite operator, hyperbolic models place features on positive-definite Riemannian manifolds, and dot-product and GAT-style attention scores use positive-definite inner products. On heterophilic graphs, where edges often signify dissimilarity or structural repulsion, that prior is a mismatch: no positive-definite form can assign a negative squared distance to a direction the labels separate. To measure the mismatch, we introduce the Graph Signature Index ($s_{\mathcal{G}}$), the inertia of a class-compatibility matrix built from label topology alone, and we prove that no value of the edge or node homophily index in $(0,1)$ rules out a negative eigenvalue. We then propose the Pseudo-Riemannian Attention Network (PRAT), whose attention logit is a signed squared pseudo-distance under a learnable diagonal metric initialized from $s_{\mathcal{G}}$. The design is diagnose-then-learn: the signature supplies a sign structure that unconstrained training keeps outside near-zero directions, and the projection learns the rest of the metric around it. Across fifteen node-classification benchmarks PRAT outperforms or matches the strongest heterophily-adapted models. A controlled ablation ties that performance to the sign structure itself: with architecture and protocol fixed, forbidding the metric to be indefinite costs accuracy on the graphs $s_{\mathcal{G}}$ marks as indefinite and leaves the others unchanged.
paper.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 41 pages, including appendix

analysis.problem_statement: Standard Graph Neural Networks impose a positive-definite geometric prior that fundamentally mismatches heterophilic graphs, where edges often represent dissimilarity or structural repulsion.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Geometric inductive bias mismatch in heterophilic graph representation learning.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper identifies a fundamental limitation in current GNNs, where positive-definite metrics fail to capture negative squared distances required for heterophilic structures. By introducing a Pseudo-Riemannian Attention Network (PRAT) that uses a learnable indefinite metric initialized via a new Graph Signature Index, it resolves this mismatch. This allows for more accurate node classification on graphs where connected nodes are dissimilar, a common scenario in real-world data like social networks or biological interactions.
